lead: Gasoline direct injection (GDI) sprays petrol straight into the combustion chamber instead of into the inlet port. The fuel arrives after the air is trapped, so the ECU decides not only how much fuel each cylinder gets but also where in the chamber it goes and at what crank angle. That lets the engine cool its charge, resist knock, raise its compression ratio and, at light load, burn a lean layered charge. Most new turbocharged petrol cars, including small Indian hatchbacks and SUVs, use it.
prereq: You need: Electronic fuel injection for sensors and pulse width, and Common rail direct injection for the rail idea.

blocks.text: A GDI fuel system has two stages. An electric pump in the tank sends petrol at about 3 to 6 bar to a high-pressure pump on the cylinder head. That pump is a single plunger driven by a lobe on the camshaft. A solenoid quantity control valve lets the unwanted part of each stroke spill back, so the pump delivers only what the rail needs. The rail feeds one injector per cylinder and carries a pressure sensor and a pressure-limiting valve. Rail pressure is roughly 50 to 200 bar in most systems and up to about 350 bar in newer ones, far below a diesel rail but fifty or more times port-injection pressure.

The injector sits in the head with its tip in the chamber, either at the side under the inlet ports or in the centre next to the spark plug. Most are solenoid multi-hole injectors; some use a piezo stack driving an outward-opening needle for a very repeatable spray. The pressure must be high for two reasons: the injector must spray against the rising cylinder pressure late in compression, and the fuel has only a few milliseconds to evaporate.

items: Tank pump: low pressure, about 3 to 6 bar.
Cam-driven high-pressure pump with quantity control valve.
Rail with pressure sensor and limiting valve.
Injector in the chamber, opened by the ECU; spark plug close by.

blocks.text: In homogeneous mode the fuel is injected early, during the intake stroke. It has the whole intake and compression strokes to mix, so the charge is uniform at about the chemically correct ratio, as with port injection. This is the mode for medium and full load, and the three-way catalyst works normally.

In stratified mode the fuel is injected late in the compression stroke. A small, ignitable rich cloud forms around the spark plug while the rest of the cylinder holds air or very lean mixture. The overall A/F can be far leaner than 14.7, so the throttle can stay wide open and the pumping loss of a throttled engine falls. The cloud must reach the plug at the right moment, and three ways of steering it are named: wall-guided (a shaped piston bowl turns the spray towards the plug), air-guided (tumble or swirl carries it) and spray-guided (the injector sits next to the plug and the spray edge itself is ignited).

blocks.text: Because lean exhaust cannot be cleaned of NOx by a three-way catalyst, stratified engines need a lean NOx trap, and many production GDI engines run homogeneous at all loads and keep direct injection for its cooling and knock benefits.

Petrol absorbs its latent heat as it evaporates. In a port-injected engine much of that heat comes from the hot port and valve; in GDI it comes from the trapped air, so the charge cools. A cooler charge is denser, so more air is trapped, and it is less prone to knock, so the compression ratio can be raised by about one ratio, for example from 10 to 11. With no fuel film on the port walls, the engine also responds faster to the throttle and starts with less excess fuel.

blocks.where: ΔT is the fall in charge temperature (K) if all the evaporation heat comes from the air; h<sub>fg</sub> is the latent heat of petrol (kJ/kg); c<sub>p</sub> is the specific heat of air, 1.005 kJ/kg K.

items: Soot and particulate number: fuel that hits the piston or liner, or has little time to mix, burns rich; many new GDI cars carry a gasoline particulate filter.
Intake valve deposits: no fuel washes the back of the inlet valves, so oil vapour from crankcase ventilation bakes on them.
Injector tip deposits change the spray; the high-pressure pump adds cost, noise and engine load.
Fuel wetting the liner can dilute the oil, and downsized turbo GDI engines can suffer low-speed pre-ignition.

examples.question: A GDI engine injects during the intake stroke at A/F = 14.7. Take the latent heat of petrol as 305 kJ/kg and c<sub>p</sub> of air as 1.005 kJ/kg K. Estimate the fall in charge temperature if all the evaporation heat comes from the air, and the gain in trapped air mass if the air would otherwise enter at 320 K and the pressure stays the same.
steps: Fuel per kg of air = 1 ÷ 14.7 = 0.0680 kg.
Heat taken from 1 kg of air = 0.0680 × 305 = 20.75 kJ.
At the same pressure, density ∝ 1/T, so the air mass rises by 320 ÷ 299.4 = 1.069, about 6.9 %.
examples.answer: The charge cools by about 21 K and traps about 7 % more air. It is an upper limit: some of the heat still comes from the walls and some fuel evaporates after the inlet valve closes.

examples.question: In stratified mode at 2000 rpm a cylinder needs 12 mg of petrol. At the chosen rail pressure the injector delivers 10 mg per millisecond. The injection must end 35° before TDC. How long is the injector open, how many crank degrees does that take, and when must it start?
examples.answer: 1.2 ms, 14.4° of crank, starting about 49° before TDC. The fuel then has only about 35° (2.9 ms) to form the cloud before TDC, which is why the spray must be fine and the pressure high.

traps: GDI is not port injection with a different name: the injector is in the chamber, the pressure is tens to hundreds of bar, and injection timing is a free choice.
Stratified does not mean the whole charge is rich. The cloud at the plug is rich enough to ignite; the cylinder as a whole is lean.
Writing that GDI keeps the inlet valves clean. It is the opposite: port injection washes the valves, GDI does not, so valve deposits are a GDI problem.
The charge-cooling estimate uses A/F to get fuel per kg of air; dividing h<sub>fg</sub> by c<sub>p</sub> alone gives an impossible 300 K drop.
A three-way catalyst cannot remove NOx from lean stratified exhaust; that is why stratified engines need a lean NOx trap.

quiz.q: State the typical fuel pressure ranges of port injection and gasoline direct injection.
quiz.a: Port injection about 3 to 4 bar; GDI about 50 to 200 bar, up to about 350 bar in newer systems.

quiz.q: Name the two main charge modes of a GDI engine and when each is injected.
quiz.a: Homogeneous: injected in the intake stroke. Stratified: injected late in the compression stroke.

quiz.q: Why does direct injection allow a higher compression ratio than port injection?
quiz.a: The fuel evaporates inside the cylinder and takes its latent heat from the trapped air, so the charge is cooler and less prone to knock; the compression ratio can be raised by about one ratio.

quiz.q: Distinguish wall-guided, air-guided and spray-guided stratification.
quiz.a: Wall-guided: the piston bowl turns the spray to the plug. Air-guided: tumble or swirl carries the fuel cloud. Spray-guided: the injector is next to the plug and the spray edge is ignited directly.

quiz.q: Repeat the charge-cooling estimate for ethanol, with A/F = 9 and latent heat 840 kJ/kg (c<sub>p</sub> 1.005 kJ/kg K).
quiz.a: Fuel per kg air = 1/9 = 0.111 kg; heat = 0.111 × 840 = 93.3 kJ; ΔT = 93.3 ÷ 1.005 = 92.9 K as an upper limit, about four and a half times the petrol value.

quiz.q: A GDI injector must deliver 15 mg at 8 mg/ms at 3000 rpm. Find the crank angle of the injection.
A GDI car shows high particulate readings only in the first minutes after a cold start. Explain why.
quiz.a: With cold walls the fuel that hits the piston and liner does not evaporate fast; it burns as rich pool fires and leaves soot. The ECU also adds fuel and may split injection to heat the catalyst. Once the walls are hot the wetted fuel evaporates and particulates fall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer systems raise rail pressure to cut particulates, and some engines combine port and direct injectors to keep the valves clean and run each where it works best. Gasoline particulate filters are now common on GDI cars to meet particle-number limits. Search for spray-guided combustion, gasoline particulate filter and low-speed pre-ignition.
